clue.text: Who's in pub besetting teetotal European?

indicators.note: to beset is to surround, so the pub goes round the other letters

parts.note: a bar is a pub

explanation.surface: Who is in the pub, crowding round a non-drinking European?
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket and baseball the side batting is 'in', so the one 'who's in' is the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: A batter is the player currently at the crease or plate, the one taking an innings.

clue.text: Incoherent talk from a loud female on feeding baby cut short

indicators.note: the letters feed into the shortened baby, going inside it
cut short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: the word baby itself, trimmed to BAB
F is forte, the musical abbreviation for loud
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side, so on gives LEG

explanation.surface: Garbled speech from a noisy woman feeding a child before stopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut short' gives BAB; A, F, F and LEG go inside it. In cricket the on side is also called the leg side.
explanation.definitionFit: Bafflegab is jargon-laden or confusing language, gobbledygook that makes no sense.

clue.text: Tool REM deployed for musical effect

indicators.note: Troops deployed are spread out into fresh positions, and the seven letters beside the word take up fresh positions too.

parts.note: the capitalised band and the implement next to it are seven letters of raw material, not a description

explanation.walkthrough: Two bands in one clue, and neither of them matters: R.E.M. is there because the letters are useful, and the effect wanted is a violinist's, not a guitarist's.
explanation.definitionFit: musical effect → TREMOLO: a tremolo is the rapid wavering repetition of a note that a player produces deliberately, so it is an effect named in the language of music.

clue.text: Dust devils? Large maybe, then small

indicators.note: A signal that the word before it is one instance of what is wanted rather than the thing itself, so a particular person of that name is being asked for.

parts.note: Eddie Large was half of Little and Large, the British comedy double act, so the surname clues a forename by example
S is the clothing-label abbreviation for small

explanation.walkthrough: Large and small read as a pair of adjectives, which is the trap: one is a comedian's surname and the other a size on a label. Little is in the grid too, at 14 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Dust devils → EDDIES: a dust devil is a whirl of air spinning debris up off the ground, which is an eddy made visible.

clue.text: Corks regularly seen around Fitzgerald's booze-filled rooms?

indicators.note: seen around means the kept letters are placed on either side of the singer's name
regularly means every other letter of the word corks is kept, the first, third and fifth

parts.note: the word corks supplies the letters that are kept
Ella Fitzgerald, the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: Wine stoppers turn up near a famous singer, presumably in rooms full of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' keeps the odd letters of Corks, CRS; 'seen around' splits them so they sit either side of Ella Fitzgerald, the jazz singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cellars are underground storerooms where wine and beer are stocked, hence playfully rooms full of booze.

clue.text: Patisserie items are wrapped in piece of cling film

indicators.note: wrapped in means the unit for are sits inside the surrounding letters
piece of means just one letter, the first, is taken from the word cling

parts.note: the first letter of cling
Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel
an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A

explanation.surface: Pastries are being wrapped up in a sheet of cling film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are' is not a verb but the metric unit of area, A; 'wrapped in' puts it inside C, the 'piece of' cling, plus KES, a classic British film.
explanation.definitionFit: Cakes are among the sweet baked goods sold in a patisserie, a pastry shop.

clue.text: Rugby player huffs over tight formation

parts.note: a lock is a second-row forward in rugby

indicators.note: over means the word for huffs is turned back to front, as this is read in reverse

parts.note: a pet is a fit of sulking, so huffs are pets

explanation.surface: A rugby forward sulks about a tight scrum formation.
explanation.walkthrough: A lock is a second-row forward in rugby; 'over' turns PETS, sulks, back to front as STEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockstep is a way of marching in close file, each person moving exactly with the one in front, so a tight formation.

clue.text: Shocking, American's scorn undermining male in support group

indicators.note: in a down clue the scorn goes under, after, the other letters
the male letter goes in the support group

parts.note: AA is Alcoholics Anonymous, a support group
zing is American slang for a cutting remark, scorn

explanation.surface: An American's disdain upsets a man at a support group meeting, shockingly.
explanation.definitionFit: Amazing means astonishing, causing great surprise, just like shocking in its loose sense.

clue.text: E.g. exhausted live stand-up comedian from Liverpool?

parts.note: e.g. means 'for example', and one everyday word does the same job in a sentence: 'say, an apple'

indicators.note: Something exhausted has had its contents used up, so the word beside it keeps only the two letters at its edges.

parts.note: the outer letters of the four-letter word, its middle emptied out

explanation.walkthrough: Alexei Sayle, the Liverpool-born comedian and actor, was a leading figure in the alternative comedy boom of the early 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: stand-up comedian from Liverpool → SAYLE: Alexei Sayle was born in the city and built his career in stand-up, so the surname names the man himself.

clue.text: More close-fitting silken pants I must wear with Romeo

indicators.note: British slang for rubbish or useless, and letters in a useless order are the ones a solver has to put right.

parts.note: six letters of raw material; the fabric is there for the surface alone
the speaker joins the mixture as the single letter used to write them
R is Romeo in the NATO spelling alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' works twice over: a garment in the surface sentence and, in the wordplay, the slang for hopeless that tells you the letters are in the wrong order.
explanation.definitionFit: More close-fitting → SLINKIER: slinky describes clothing cut to cling to the body, so the comparative is a garment fitting closer still.

clue.text: Massive fan of sci-fi endorsing Banks

indicators.note: To bank a thing is to stow it away for keeping, so the capitalised surname is quietly saying the letters are stored inside the words in front of it.

parts.note: five consecutive letters run straight across the space between the two words

explanation.walkthrough: Iain Banks wrote literary novels and, as Iain M. Banks, science fiction, so the capital letter looks like a tribute to a writer rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Massive fan → FIEND: a fiend for something is an addict of it — a fresh-air fiend, a crossword fiend — enthusiasm rather than the devil.

clue.text: Be attracted to eccentric with a will

parts.note: to be attracted to somebody is to like them
an eccentric person is crazy in the mild, affectionate sense of the word

explanation.walkthrough: Two everyday synonyms laid end to end, and the join is invisible because the sentence reads so smoothly as a description of somebody's temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: with a will → LIKE CRAZY: doing a job with a will means throwing energy at it, and doing it like crazy is the same idea in slang.

clue.text: John Cleese's latest two characters complete special BBC radio show

parts.note: john is slang for a toilet, a loo

indicators.note: latest two characters means only the final pair of letters of the surname survive, everything before them dropped

parts.note: the comedian's surname, Cleese, whose letters are cut down to its closing pair
to complete something is to end it, so completes, here ends

explanation.surface: John Cleese's two most recent roles round off a special BBC radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'John' is not Cleese's first name here but slang for a toilet; 'latest two characters' keeps just SE, the final pair of letters of Cleese.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose Ends is a long-running BBC Radio 4 chat and arts programme hosted on Saturday evenings.

clue.text: Sleeps around, initially eschewing drug

indicators.note: around means the word for sleeps is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: to kip is to sleep, so sleeps are kips

indicators.note: initially means only the opening letter of eschewing is taken

parts.note: the first letter of eschewing

explanation.surface: Someone who sleeps around starts off by avoiding drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sleeps around' suggests promiscuity, but 'around' reverses the word for sleeps, giving SPIK; 'initially' then adds the first letter of eschewing.
explanation.definitionFit: To spike a drink is to secretly add a drug or alcohol to it, so spike is a verb meaning to dope.

clue.text: Turn over waffle

parts.note: your turn in a game is your go
the two prepositions swap freely — you tell somebody over the phone or on the phone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn over' looks like an instruction to reverse something, which is the trap in a three-word clue; it is really two separate synonyms, one word each.
explanation.definitionFit: waffle → GO ON: to go on is to keep talking well past the point of interest, which is what waffling amounts to.

clue.text: Pinch Mini

definitions.meaning: a pinch of salt is the amount you can hold between finger and thumb, which is to say a very small quantity
a mini skirt or a mini break is a small version of the thing, so the prefix is the same idea again

explanation.walkthrough: Two words of clue and no wordplay at all: the setter's economy is the joke, and Syd Little of Little and Large is looking across at 3 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Pinch and Mini both point at smallness: a pinch is the little you can hold in two fingers, and mini is the prefix meaning little in size.

clue.text: Like a rough gust, high on the rocks

indicators.note: A marriage or a ship on the rocks has come to pieces, and letters in pieces have to be put back together in a new order.

parts.note: eight letters of raw material: the weather and the state of mind are surface only

explanation.walkthrough: A rough, in older British usage, is a hooligan or a ruffian, which is what makes the adjective fair; 'on the rocks' is the drink the surface is pouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Like a rough → THUGGISH: a rough is a British term for a violent hooligan, and thuggish is the adjective for behaving as one does.

clue.text: Room accommodating squatters?

parts.note: read straight, this is a building somebody has moved into without permission, and that housing-page picture is what the clue wants you to see first; the setter's reading makes them exercisers instead: a squat is the knees-bent lift done with a barbell, and the people doing it need a hall with equipment in it

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to unpick here. The whole clue is the definition, and the joke is that the second reading of 'squatters' is entirely straight-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Room accommodating squatters → GYM: the answer is the room set aside for people doing squats, so the pun is itself the definition and nothing is assembled.

clue.text: Habit of guy, beginning to moan when interrupted by flipping alarm

indicators.note: when interrupted by means the reversed alarm breaks into the middle of the letters before it

parts.note: a guy is a man

indicators.note: beginning to means only the first letter of moan is used

parts.note: the first letter of moan

indicators.note: flipping means the word for alarm is turned over and read backwards

parts.note: a siren is an alarm

explanation.surface: A man's habit is to start moaning whenever an alarm goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to' takes M from moan to follow MAN; 'flipping' reverses SIREN to NERIS, and 'when interrupted by' puts that inside, giving MAN-NERIS-M.
explanation.definitionFit: A mannerism is a habitual gesture or way of speaking peculiar to a person, a personal habit.

clue.text: Beatles movie mostly set on island somewhere in Finland

parts.note: Help! is the band's 1965 film, and it gives up its final letter
the sun sets, or sinks, below the horizon — the same movement under either verb
I is the map-maker's abbreviation for island

explanation.walkthrough: 'Set on island' reads as a film's location, which is the surface's job; the wordplay takes the words one at a time, a synonym and then an abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in Finland → HELSINKI: it is the country's capital and largest city, so the vague definition is fair by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Height of Boeing occasionally overlooked

indicators.note: Skipping a letter here and there is what this asks for: read the word through and pass over every second one.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters of the aircraft maker, with the others passed over

explanation.walkthrough: A ben is a mountain peak in Scotland — Ben Nevis is the tallest of them — so the three letters name a height instead of measuring one.
explanation.definitionFit: Height → BEN: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, the one in Ben Nevis, so it names a high place rather than a measurement.

clue.text: Scored ten at Old Trafford in the end — fantastic!

indicators.note: fantastic suggests something wild, so the letters are rearranged
the end letter of Trafford

parts.note: its last letter gives D

explanation.surface: A striker hit ten at Manchester United's ground, a fantastic finish.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Trafford is Manchester United's football ground, but here 'Old' and 'Trafford' are split; 'Scored' means written in musical notation.
explanation.definitionFit: Music that has been scored is written down in musical notation, which is what notated means.

clue.text: Roasting chicken, having removed its head

indicators.note: The head of a word is the letter it starts with, and this says to take that letter off before using the rest.

parts.note: chicken means cowardly, and a cowardly person is fearful

explanation.walkthrough: Roasting a chicken is the picture, and both halves of it are false: the roasting is verbal and the chicken is a coward rather than a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Roasting → EARFUL: a roasting is a severe telling-off, and an earful is as much of one as a listener can take at a time.

clue.text: Youth essentially brightening poet's evening

indicators.note: The essence of a word, for a setter, is the letter sitting exactly at its centre — here the sixth of eleven.

parts.note: the middle letter of the eleven, six in from either end
e'en is the poetic contraction of evening, the one preserved in Hallowe'en

explanation.walkthrough: Poets' contractions are a standing crossword resource, worth learning as a set: e'en for evening, o'er for over, ne'er for never.
explanation.definitionFit: Youth → TEEN: a teen is a person in their teenage years, and youth names the same person by the stage of life they are at.

clue.text: Unpredictable Clapton perhaps covering Supergrass?

indicators.note: The example flag: the guitarist is one man with that first name and not the only one, so his forename is what is being clued.
To cover a thing is to lie over it from both sides, so the name opens and takes three letters inside.

parts.note: Eric Clapton the guitarist gives up his first name; the surname is only there to point at him
a supergrass is British slang for an informer who names many others at once, and a rat is the same idea in one syllable

explanation.walkthrough: Supergrass were a Britpop band, which is why they sit capitalised beside a guitarist; the wordplay wants the police-informer sense instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Unpredictable → ERRATIC: something erratic wanders off course without warning, so nobody can say what it will do next.

clue.text: McCartney possibly excellent right away

indicators.note: Away is the instruction to take a thing out: whatever it names goes missing from the word in front of it.

parts.note: the word here means excellent — literally 'of the stars', from the Latin for star, then figuratively outstanding
R is the crossword shorthand for right, and it is the letter that leaves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' reads as immediately, which is the trap: the two words are separate instructions. Stella McCartney, Paul's daughter, is a fashion designer.
explanation.definitionFit: McCartney possibly → STELLA: Stella McCartney the designer is one bearer of the surname, so 'possibly' marks a definition by example rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Son finishing off dull hour in school lesson

indicators.note: This says where a letter goes rather than which letter it is: the son is sent to the back of the queue.

parts.note: a mat finish is a dull one, the paint that does not shine
h is the abbreviation for hour
S is the standard single letter for son

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dull' wants the paint-tin sense, spelled with one T. The word that follows the son is not part of him — it is the instruction about where he goes.
explanation.definitionFit: school lesson → MATHS: it is the timetable name British schools give the subject, so the definition points at a period in the day rather than at the discipline.

clue.text: Tidy mess made by Englishman in Australia, as it were

indicators.note: mess made by means the letters of the Australian word for an Englishman are jumbled

parts.note: Pom is Australian slang for an English person
as it were points to the remaining word of the phrase, the adverb up, which completes the expression

explanation.surface: Tidy up the mess some Englishman made in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess made by' jumbles POM, the Australian slang for an English person, to MOP; UP finishes the phrase, the setter's 'as it were' owning to the looseness.
explanation.definitionFit: To mop up is to clean up spilt liquid or remaining bits, so to tidy.

clue.text: Get a shirt undone — one buttoned-up

indicators.note: Something undone has come apart, and letters that have come apart have to be fastened together again in another order.

parts.note: nine letters of raw material; the garment belongs to the surface only

explanation.walkthrough: The surface undoes a shirt and the definition does it back up, which is the joke: the buttoned-up person of the second half is the mean or repressed sort.
explanation.definitionFit: one buttoned-up → TIGHT-ARSE: calling somebody buttoned-up says they are clenched about money or pleasure, which is exactly the accusation the blunter word makes.

clue.text: Weak and ultimately disappointing cup of tea

parts.note: weak tea is thin, and the sense carries over to a weak argument as well

indicators.note: Ultimately points at the very last letter of the word beside it, the one it closes on.

parts.note: the last letter of the adjective

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the idiom, not the drink: 'not my cup of tea' means not what I care for, and the setter hides it behind a weak brew.
explanation.definitionFit: cup of tea → THING: in the idiom 'not my cup of tea', the phrase means the sort of pursuit a person enjoys — what somebody would call their thing.

clue.text: Broadcast satisfactory, assume a haughty manner

parts.note: to broadcast a programme is to put it on air
S is the grade meaning satisfactory on a school report

explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' is a favourite anagram signal, and that is the trap here: it is a plain synonym, and the phrase it hands over is three words long.
explanation.definitionFit: assume a haughty manner → PUT ON AIRS: to put on airs is to adopt a grandeur you have no claim to, so the definition is the idiom's plain meaning.

clue.text: Partly flat, Hindu's wooden weapon

indicators.note: Only part of what follows is wanted, and the part in question is a run of letters sitting inside it untouched.

parts.note: five letters run straight on across the comma and into the next word

explanation.walkthrough: The comma and the apostrophe are the camouflage: punctuation counts for nothing in the letters, so the run reads through them as if they were not there.
explanation.definitionFit: wooden weapon → LATHI: a lathi is the heavy bamboo baton carried by Indian police, so it is a wooden weapon in the plainest sense.

clue.text: Party brought about noise next to golf course

indicators.note: brought about means the party's letters are turned around and read backwards

parts.note: the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland
din is noise
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A political party arranged noise near a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought about' sounds like 'caused' but reverses DUP to PUD; 'course' is not the golf course but a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pudding is the dessert course of a British meal, served after the main dish.

clue.text: Neither finishing much, each having twisted part of gut

indicators.note: twisted means the letters remaining from the two shortened words are wound into a new order
neither, read with finishing, means the first word, much, loses its last letter
finishing, read with neither, means the second word, each, likewise loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Neither of two things gets finished, each one having a twisted gut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neither finishing' cuts the last letter from both much and each, leaving MUC and EAC; 'twisted' rearranges those six letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The caecum is the pouch at the start of the large intestine, a section of the bowel.
